This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

—Grace Huckins

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.

“We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it .

The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

—James O’Donnell

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape.

Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback.

The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Find out why .

This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

+ Huang hired a PR firm known for handling sex scandals last year. ( Wired $)

+ Hackers are shifting to manipulating physical equipment. ( Axios )
+ Is your smart kitchen next? ( Wired $)

The main driver is energy supply constraints. ( New Scientist $)

Quote of the day

—Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at ​Bernstein, tells Reuters why it will be so difficult to replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.

One More Thing

China wants to restore the sea with high-tech marine ranches

Just a short ferry ride from the Chinese port city of Yantai sits Genghai No. 1, a strange offshore complex that combines a tourist attraction with an industrial fish farm. It even has a seven-story visitor center shaped like a cartoon starfish. But its main purpose is to breed fish and release them into the ocean.

Genghai is part of China’s ambitious marine ranching program. Since 2015, the country has built 169 demonstration ranches and released at least 167 billion juvenile fish and shellfish. But the approach has also proved controversial.

Dive into China’s divisive plans to restore the seas with marine ranches .

articles.title: Evolving metal extraction processes
articles.excerpt: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting…
articles.fullText:
The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible.

Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize.

Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?

EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted:

“We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.”

A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem

As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on.

Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience.

That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions.

Beyond optimization

For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways.

The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential.

Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness.

Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology

Source : Outokumpu

Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT.

“The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste.

Innovation happens at the boundaries

EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies.

Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work.

“Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production.

Building a technology platform

A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications.

Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point.

“The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains.

That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing.

The future of materials companies

The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise.

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible.

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives.

The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030. Beyond producing low-CO 2 , chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum.

The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today?

The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on.

Read more about this topic and hear more from Caspar Stinn and Antoine Allanore .

This content was produced by Outokumpu. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

articles.title: Operation Santa Claus unlocks HK's spirit of giving
articles.excerpt: Operation Santa Claus (OSC), a long-running annual fundraising campaign, officially launched on Tuesday to offer care and support for those…
articles.fullText:
Operation Santa Claus (OSC), a long-running annual fundraising campaign, officially launched on Tuesday to offer care and support for those in need across the city.

Co-organised by RTHK and the South China Morning Post (SCMP),
the fundraising event themed “Unlock the City’s Spirit of Giving” this year will support 13 local organisations that focus on serving children, the youth, elderly, people with disabilities, and mental health challenges in the community.

At the launch ceremony, Director of Broadcasting Angelina Kwan noted the campaign has been helping people in need since 1988.

“Through good times and difficult times, this campaign has continued. Year after year, people across our city have given their time, their energy and their support,” she said.

“That consistency is what gives Operation Santa Claus its strong reputation in town.”

“This city’s generosity has grown with each passing year, reaching hundreds of charitable projects and tens of thousands of lives,” Tammy Tam, SCMP's publisher said, noting that the generosity reached new heights last year when the deadly inferno at Wang Fuk Court occurred.

“My deepest gratitude also goes to every donor. Whether you gave a little or a lot, you made this campaign what it is.”

The launch ceremony featured a musical performance by singer Miriam Ma, along with young talents Yuet Ng and Yat Ng, to showcase how the smallest acts of courage and kindness can inspire the community.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Sino-US forum held in HK ahead of Apec summit
articles.excerpt: Global leaders across various fields will gather in Hong Kong ahead of the Apec leaders' summit in Shenzhen to discuss…
articles.fullText:
Global leaders across various fields will gather in Hong Kong ahead of the Apec leaders' summit in Shenzhen to discuss how Sino-US relations can be reshaped in search of long-term stability and cooperation.

The annual US-China Hong Kong Forum will be held between November 15 and 17.

James Chau, president of the organisers China-United States Exchange Foundation, said dozens of speakers would be joining the event, including former vice foreign minister Cui Tiankai, members of the Nixon and Bush families from the US, and former Thailand prime minister Abhisit Vejjajiva.

“Through this forum we also bring regional perspectives into the discussion," Chau said.

"So we've got Asean, for example, represented by Thailand, but also by Singapore. The [Sino-US] relationship affects more than two countries, so there's always that temptation to look at our work simply through the bilateral lens of China and the United States.

“I wish it was like that because it seems very tidy, neat and easy to follow. But, in fact, everything that these two countries do and don't do, what they think and what they consider, is going to impact over eight billion people all around the world.”

More than 300 participants will take part in the open forum on the second day, among them a group of university students from around the world.

“Having young people in the room who are 18 to 25 years old who come from phenomenal schools of public policy and who would have spent part of the private sessions with us and then into the public sessions, we want them to ask the very first question during the audience Q&A to keep those leaders on the stage very sharp,” Chau said.

The Apec summit will be held on November 18-19 in Shenzhen.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Tech gains, oil price falls lift HK, mainland markets
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong and mainland stocks closed higher on Tuesday, led by AI supply chain shares, as an overnight rally on…

Hong Kong and mainland stocks closed higher on Tuesday, led by AI supply chain shares, as an overnight rally on Wall Street and sliding oil prices lifted risk sentiment across Asia.

The benchmark Hang Seng Index closed 108 points, or 0.4 percent, higher at 24,557 on turnover of HK$178.17 billion.

The tech index rose 43 points, or 1.1 percent, to 4,084 while the China enterprises index crept five points, or 0.1 percent, up to 8,265.

Optical communication giant Zhongji Innolight jumped nine percent while Wuxi AppTec rose up to five percent before paring gains after the Pentagon removed the biotechnology company from its list of Chinese military companies.

Mainland chip firms Suzhou Denglin Technology and Jiangsu Xinde Semiconductor Technology made mixed trading debuts after raising a combined HK$2.36 billion in initial public offerings.

AI chip designer Suzhou Denglin ended HK$18, or 7.79 percent, down at HK$213 while semiconductor packager and tester Jiangsu Xinde was HK$2.52, or 28 percent, up at HK$11.40.

On the mainland, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index inched up just under three points, or 0.08 percent, to end at 3,663.

The Shenzhen Component Index was 96 points, or 0.86 percent, higher at 11,241 while the ChiNext Index was 35 points, or 1.46 percent, up at 2,494.

Chip supply chain shares across Asia climbed, tracking an overnight rally on Wall Street that saw the Nasdaq jump 2.7 percent.

The 5G Communication Index rose 2.6 percent, leading gains onshore, while the tech-focused Star50 Index was up nearly one percent.

Non-ferrous metal shares edged up 0.1 percent as gold prices rebounded this month on falling oil prices.

The CSI Energy Index fell 2.6 percent, with PetroChina down 6.3 percent.

China's trade surplus surged past US$1 trillion in the first 10 months as a global race to build AI infrastructure buoyed sales of high-tech products and helped offset weak domestic demand, a dynamic likely to sharpen tensions with major trading partners.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei climbed up by 1,684 points, or 2.87 percent, to end at 60,459, extending its rebound from a tech-led selloff on Friday as AI-related stocks surged.

The broader Topix was up 75 points, or 1.98 percent, at 3,893.

In Seoul, the Kospi closed up 220 points, or 4.39 percent, at 5,239 in a sharp rebound from nine-month lows as chipmakers tracked overnight gains in US tech stocks. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: 'SZ, HK should join hands to grow external trade'
articles.excerpt: As Shenzhen's maritime logistics industry has taken off in recent years, a senior official at one of the world's busiest…
articles.fullText:
As Shenzhen's maritime logistics industry has taken off in recent years, a senior official at one of the world's busiest container terminals said Hong Kong still had much to offer as the nation forges closer ties with the world.

Yantian Port, in eastern Shenzhen, is a vital gateway between the nation's manufacturing engine and global markets.

It handles more than one-third of Guangdong's foreign trade and a quarter of the country's container exports to the United States.

According to the Shenzhen municipal government, the deep-water port handled 16.1 million TEUs, or twenty-foot equivalent units, in 2025, representing a 7.1 percent year-on-year increase.

Lawrence Shum, managing director of Yantian, a subsidiary of Hutchison Ports, said the terminal operates nearly 100 international routes on a weekly basis.

Fifty-three of those routes are linked to Apec economies.

"Since the start of this year, we have added 14 new routes to and from Apec economies, further expanding our international network and fostering regional trade," he said.

"According to the customs figures, Shenzhen continues to lead the country in both imports and exports to Apec economies. We even set a record in the first nine months of this year, with a trade value of 3.23 trillion yuan, a 40 percent jump."

Shenzhen is the host of this year's Apec leaders' summit scheduled for November 18 and 19.

Shum explained that Yantian had a unique advantage over other Shenzhen ports when handling shipments from inland regions.

"Yantian houses Shenzhen's only railway that reaches directly into the port area. Through sea‑rail intermodal transport, port services can be extended to inland regions such as the southwest and central areas, making it more convenient for enterprises in Chengdu and Chongqing and bringing them closer to international markets," he said.

Under Shenzhen's 15th Five-Year Plan, Yantian is to strengthen cooperation with Hong Kong's Kwai Tsing Container Terminals.

Shum said six daily vessel trips between the two ports mean cargo can arrive at its destination in about six to eight hours.

"For inland foreign trade enterprises, transportation time can be more stable, more efficient, and more environmentally friendly. Shenzhen and Hong Kong can further tap into inland cargo trade ... and achieve a win‑win for the three regions," Shum said.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: No internet, no advance warning: 11 killed in Myanmar military bombing in Sagaing
articles.excerpt: Civilians in war zones are left vulnerable as Starlink internet becomes scarce after scam center crackdown.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Burmese
It was just before noon on Saturday. Three gyrocopters flew low as they approached Nyaung Pin Lay village. A school and surrounding residential area was bombed. Eleven were killed, including four children.
A resident told RFA that although the local People’s Defense Forces (PDF) received a tip that the Myanmar military would bomb the school, the warning could not reach them in time due to the lack of internet in the village.
“Information that this would be bombed was sent online to everyone. They did inform us,” the Kani Township resident told RFA on the condition of anonymity for security reasons.
“But because there was no Starlink communication, casualties were high as a result. About a month ago in Nat La Po village, when we got the exact location that would be bombed and cleared the area, there were no casualties. That was fortunate. But now, even though we got the location to be bombed, communication was cut off.”
A May 25, 2025, photo shows a Starlink sign at an internet cafe in Demoso, Myanmar.
(AFP) In Myanmar, home to the world’s longest-running civil war, the military-appointed government has cut off phone lines and internet communications in over 40 percent of townships nationwide. Locals, civil society groups, and revolutionary forces tell RFA that they rely on Starlink — acquiring the devices through unofficial and often expensive channels — as a lifeline for information.
In October 2025, SpaceX announced the disabling of over 2,500 Starlink kits in Myanmar to crack down on transnational cyber-scam syndicates operating along the Thai-Myanmar border. Subsequent restrictions by SpaceX on unregistered units bought outside of Myanmar have shut down countless others.
Since June, more than 20 percent of Starlink internet devices used in Myanmar have had their services cut off, according to a report released on Oct. 23 by the group Athan.
Local residents and human rights activists told RFA that this has created a crisis for the survival of civilians in areas of intense civil conflict.
A Myanmar government photo taken on Oct. 20, 2025, shows seized Starlink devices during a raid on the KK Park online scam center in Myawaddy.
(Myanmar Military Information Team via AFP) “The military cutting off phone lines and internet connections from the start was intentionally aimed at concealing human rights violations they commit and restricting people’s freedom of expression,” said Joy, a research director at Athan, a non-profit organization for the Freedom of Expression Movement in Myanmar.
“If Starlink also stops providing services to Myanmar and cuts connections, emergency humanitarian aid, air strike alerts, news regarding military columns, and natural disaster warnings for these local residents will stop immediately.”
According to a report titled “Dead Air” released by Athan on October 23, the communication cut-off directly affects the lives and safety of people in conflict-affected regions as they can no longer receive warnings about airstrikes and military movements, medical aid, or updates on family members’ safety and evacuation routes.
RFA contacted Khaing Khaing Soe, spokesperson for the military-appointed president’s office, regarding when internet and phone lines might be restored. She instead referred RFA to the Ministry of Digital Development and Communications.
Now, not only Starlink devices used by scam operations are being shut down, but Starlink connections used by civilians have also been suspended starting in June this year, with more than 20 percent of devices cut off by October, according to Athan. Consequently, regions like Sagaing, Mandalay, Magway, Rakhine, Kayah State, and other areas experiencing severe conflict were directly affected, Athan’s report states.
RFA contacted SpaceX regarding the impact on civilians in regions where the internet has been cut off, but has not received a response at the time of publication.
“Some of our Starlink devices were disabled. This has caused a lot of trouble for us,” said Aye Myint Aung Aung, Head of the Department of Humanitarian Assistance and Emergency Management under the Mandalay Regional Interim Administrative Council.
“On the other hand, whether it’s our civilians, revolutionary groups, or those leading and operating the administrative mechanism in revolutionary forces, everyone relies on Starlink. As access to information becomes more restricted, limitations on civilian safety also increase. I would define this as a very major challenge for us.”
In Kayah State, Deputy Minister of Defense for the Karenni State Government Khu Daniel told RFA that Starlink connections are being shut down one by one, raising concerns.
“For the public and for the youth currently fighting in battle, it will become a cause for concern,” he said.
A Sept. 17, 2025, photo shows people on a balcony of a building with what appears to be Starlink satellite dishes on the roof in the KK Park complex in Myawaddy, Myanmar.
(Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP) Khun Chit Htoo, who is assisting refugees in the Karenni Region, said that if all Starlink services are shut down, it could have a severe impact on humanitarian aid operations.
“Our current work relies on internet connectivity as well as donors. Since we connect online, we are very concerned,” said Khun Chit Htoo.
“We will face a situation where we can no longer help needy civilians receive the support they really need across all aspects of coordination. If there is no internet line left, I believe we stand to lose a lot because of this single connection.”
While welcoming and supporting the shutdown of Starlink internet lines used by online scam operations to crack down on scam syndicates, 317 civil society organizations issued a statement on July 17 expressing deep concern over potential negative impacts if all Starlink terminals nationwide are shut down.
According to an October 23 report by the Myanmar Internet Project, an organization monitoring internet shutdowns and conflicts, there were 581 military airstrikes that killed at least 353 civilians in the three months from July to September 2026, with 562 of those attacks occurring in areas where internet service was cut off.
Translated by Nayrein Kyaw. Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: China says trade surplus surpassed US$1tn in October
articles.excerpt: China's trade surplus exceeded US$1 trillion for a second year in a row, according to official data released on Tuesday…
articles.fullText:
China's trade surplus exceeded US$1 trillion for a second year in a row, according to official data released on Tuesday.

The nation's foreign trade in goods maintained strong growth momentum in the first 10 months of 2026, with imports posting especially robust gains, according to official data.

Total imports and exports grew 20 percent year on year over the period, accelerating from 18.8 percent in the first nine months, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC).

Exports jumped 35.2 percent year-on-year to US$412.3 billion last month, according to the GAC, while imports in October expanded 41.6 percent to US$307.1 billion.

Between January and October, the country logged a US$1.04 trillion trade surplus, even as the trade surplus narrowed last month to US$105.3 billion from US$133.5 billion in September as imports picked up pace.

Analysts expect China to surpass the record US$1.2 trillion surplus it hit last year.

“We expect Chinese exports to stay strong for the rest of this year, led by electronics and autos,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics.

Meanwhile, exports to the United States surged 32.9 percent last month, the GAC data showed.

The figures come ahead of another meeting between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen next week.

The two have navigated a shaky truce to a trade war since their meeting in October 2025. They also met twice this year.

Beijing on Monday officially announced the extension of a trade truce with Washington due to expire on November 10 by two months, but said last week that expanding its purchases of US farm goods would hinge on the implementation of their agreed reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement.

"The risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will remain elevated in 2027, particularly as Chinese manufacturers continue expanding their presence in overseas markets," said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China.

Greater reliance on exports, however, leaves China's economy increasingly exposed to any slowdown in global demand.

Much of the strength in exports this year has been fuelled by a global push to expand AI infrastructure.

"The outlook for exports depends on how long the AI boom will last," Macquarie analysts wrote.

They expect China's exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before starting to slow from the first quarter of 2027. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: US military surrenders in court fight with WuXi AppTec
articles.excerpt: The US military has removed mainland biotechnology company WuXi AppTec from its list of Chinese military companies, according to a…
articles.fullText:
The US military has removed mainland biotechnology company WuXi AppTec from its list of Chinese military companies, according to a government posting.

The deputy secretary of defence made the determination on Monday in light of a federal court in Washington barring the department from enforcing the designation, the posting said.

The ruling came in a lawsuit WuXi AppTec filed after the Pentagon added it to the list, saying its designation was arbitrary, capricious, unsupported by the facts and "the product of political pressure".

The US military's headquarters at the Pentagon expanded its blacklist of alleged "Chinese military companies" on June 8 to 188 entities.

"This decision relieves the company from further adverse consequences of the 1260H designation," WuXi AppTec said in a filing to the Hong Kong bourse on Tuesday morning, referring to the list that is kept under section 1260H of a US defence law.

"We remain committed to serving our customers and enabling the lifesaving and life-improving medicines they make for patients," the company added. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK, regional markets get a bump from Wall St gains
articles.excerpt: Asian stocks rose on Tuesday as a drop in oil prices after US President Donald Trump said he planned to…
articles.fullText:
Asian stocks rose on Tuesday as a drop in oil prices after US President Donald Trump said he planned to hold off on new military strikes against Iran lifted sentiment ahead of US inflation data that could sway the near-term interest rate outlook.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index opened up 172 points, or 0.7 percent, at 24,621.

The China enterprises index rose 38 points, or 0.47 percent, to 8,298 while the tech index climbed 31 points, or 0.78 percent, to 4,072.

Two chip-sector firms debuted in Hong Kong, with AI chip designer Suzhou Denglin Technology falling into loss territory at the start of trading and semiconductor packager and tester Jiangsu Xinde Semiconductor Technology making a much stronger debut.

Across the border, the Shanghai Composite Index opened up 21 points, or 0.58 percent, at 3,682.

The Shenzhen Component Index put on 167 points, or 1.51 percent, to open at 11,313 while the ChiNext Index rose 59 points, or 2.44 percent, to 2,518.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei opened 596 points, or 1.02 percent, higher at 59,372 and was 1,725 points or almost three percent higher at one stage before noon.

In Seoul, the Kospi surged 228 points, or 4.55 percent, to open at 5,247 amid gains for its heavyweight chipmakers – 3.74 percent for Samsung Electronics and 5.28 percent for SK Hynix.

The gains came as Brent crude futures were hovering at their lowest levels since early September, well below US$100 per barrel, as investors pinned their hopes on possible talks between the United States and Iran.

They were last down one percent at US$91.56 a barrel.

The US-Israeli war with Iran, which erupted at the end of February, has stoked inflationary concerns across the globe, spurring major central banks to raise rates in recent months.

Nick Twidale, chief market strategist at ATFX Global, said the latest developments offered hope that an end to the conflict could be approaching, but there was still a considerable gap between diplomacy and a lasting peace agreement.

"The risk now is that markets have moved too far, too quickly... any indication that negotiations are faltering could see a substantial rebound in prices as traders rapidly rebuild the geopolitical risk premium," he said.

The slump in oil prices eased inflation worries and helped lift stocks after last week's rout as a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections fed concerns that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade.

On Monday, the S&P 500 clocked its biggest one-day jump since April, closing up 2.35 percent while the Nasdaq closed 2.7 percent higher, its best day in over four months.

"We believe resets in expectations are healthy, and the AI trade appears to be working through a reset of its own at the moment," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise.

Earnings reports due this week from tech companies such as CoreWeave, a barometer of investor anxiety over AI, will be another test for markets as investors fret about the cost of the AI buildout.

Saglimbene said Anthropic's prospective IPO could be an important test of investor confidence.

Market focus remains on Nvidia after the second-most valuable company in the world said its board was probing whether CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation.

A media report alleged he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.

Huang has said he was unfaithful to his wife.

Shares of Nvidia, which is due to report earnings next week, fell 4.2 percent.

Daniel Morgan, a portfolio manager at Synovus Trust who holds Nvidia shares, said certain personalities in the technology space were so intertwined with the success of the company it was hard to separate the two.

"But the companies can still be successful long after the original founders have taken on a lesser role," he said, adding he remained confident that Nvidia would continue to maintain its lead in the GPU AI chip market even if Huang was forced to step down to a lesser role.

All eyes will be on US inflation data later in the day, with prices likely to have increased at a moderate pace in October, economists said, and remaining stubbornly high enough for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates next month.

Traders are pricing in an 84 percent chance of a rate hike next month versus 74 percent a week earlier, a CME FedWatch tool showed after a blowout October jobs report on Friday. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: A trip to the South Korean seaside for glimpses of my North Korean hometown
articles.excerpt: Escapee Park Sol-ji often gets homesick for the port city of Chongjin. A beach day in Busan comes close.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
Park Sol-ji stared out over the water at Gwangalli Beach with the iconic Gwangan Bridge in the distance, just above the horizon. South Korea’s touristy second largest city of Busan is a drastic change from heavily industrialized Chongjin – her hometown in North Korea. But both cities are large ports on the eastern side of the peninsula, and the sand, the breeze, and the smell of the sea reminds her of home.
“I love looking at the sea, and coming here whenever I miss my hometown is a big part of it,” she told Radio Free Asia Nov. 3. “Also, coming to the seaside makes me feel like I can finally breathe. I think I like it because it gives me such a sense of liberation.”
Park Sol-ji is a pseudonym she is using for safety reasons. Sol-ji fled North Korea 19 years ago when she was 20 years old, arriving in South Korea the following year. Adjusting to life in the fast-paced South was jarring. Though she tried her best to blend in among South Korean 20-somethings , it would all come crashing down whenever she spoke with her unmistakable North Korean accent.
She often found the degree of change in her life to be overwhelming, and she longed to return home, but that was now impossible. In times like that a trip to the sea would always remind her just enough of home to boost her spirits.
These days, she’s shed the accent and looks about the same as everyone else, but she still gets homesick and often travels to the seaside.
A map showing the locations of Chongjin, North Korea and Busan, South Korea.
(RFA) Busan is very different from Chongjin. Though both cities are industrialized ports, the South Korean city has – over many decades – invested in travel infrastructure and branded itself as a global tourist destination.
According to tourism statistics compiled by the Busan city government, more than 3.93 million foreign tourists have already visited Busan this year alone. CNN introduced Busan as “Asia’s Next Coastal City,” and Expedia selected Busan as the only Korean destination among its “Top 10 Destinations of the Year for 2027.”
But for Sol-ji, it’s not the glitz and glamor she’s coming for. She is here to take in the memories of the seaside of her childhood, where she played in the sand with her friends and spent precious moments with her family.
Memories roll in with the rising tide
Though the forecast called for cloudy weather, Gwangalli Beach had quite a few visitors from midday, perhaps due to the unexpectedly clear sky. Couples were taking photos with the sea as a backdrop, groups of noisy students on a field trip made their way across the sand, and foreign tourists walked barefoot. Everyone had smiles on their faces. Gwangalli Beach is well known as a romantic spot where the blue sea harmonizes with the spectacular night view of the Gwangan Bridge.
Sol-ji slowly surveyed the seascape and her face lit up as she spoke of the days she and her family would break out a large cauldron, build a fire, catch fish, and cook eojuk, a type of spicy fish porridge. She also remembered how she and her friends used to play by pulling up seaweed to gather in makeshift nets made of their extra clothes. Although these were ordinary childhood games, looking back now, they were moments she can never have again. To her, the sea is a landscape she longs for, as well as a place where she finds solace for her wounds.
“I even dreamt of returning to Chongjin because I missed my hometown, but even in the dream, seeing my dyed hair and decorated nails, I thought I would get caught,” she said. North Korea is notorious for fashion police who crack down on “capitalist” looks like dyed hair, colored nails, blue jeans, clothing with English words and phrases, and other no-nos. In South Korea, Sol-ji is free to dress how she wants to, but that does not erase her longing.
“I really do want to go back just once.”
The old village in the hills
Prior to visiting the beach, Sol-ji had started the day with a train ride to Busan Station, disembarking in the morning. The first spot on her itinerary was Gamcheon Culture Village, a 10-minute taxi ride away. The village started as a ramshackle town built up in the hills for laborers, and it expanded greatly with the swell of refugees fleeing to Busan from the advancing North Korean army in the opening weeks of the 1950-53 Korean War. In recent years the village was painstakingly restored through cultural preservation and beautification projects.
These days, tourists flock to its narrow meandering streets, attracted by the colorfully painted houses, many of which have been converted to shops, cafes and mini-museums. Near the high point of the village sits a colorful statue of the Little Prince, presiding over a space dedicated to the mythos presented in Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s world-renowned novella.
A statue of the Little Prince and the fox at the Little Prince House in Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, South Korea.
(Saha-gu Office via korea.net) Today, the tourists have come in force. More often than not, passersby who came for the village’s unique artsy flair will be speaking in a language other than Korean.
While most tourists are browsing the shops, ordering refreshments, or taking in one of the museums, Sol-ji slowly looks around the alley, finally focusing on a clothesline in the courtyard of one house. She noticed three or four items of clothing hanging on a single line, swaying in the breeze. It was this evidence that people actually live here that conjured up the feelings of her childhood.
“People here hang their laundry on clotheslines like that. It’s exactly the same in North Korea,” she said. She explained that in North Korea some families have washing machines, but rolling blackouts are common in most places, so people still have to do laundry by hand.
“So here they also dry their laundry in the sun,” she said. “Knowing this is quite heartwarming.”
In another area of town she operated a manual pump that once drew water out of the ground. She said it made her think of her grandmother’s house in Chongjin.
Sol-ji walked along, looking around every corner of the alley. Though sun-dried laundry and the hand pump might be similar details, the nature of this town, built up on a hillside, would never make sense in Chongjin, she said.
Park Sol-ji, visits Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “There aren’t many houses on slopes like this in Chongjin. It costs a lot of money to build roads and houses up to these inclines,” she said. “Instead, there are many fields on these mountain slopes. It is land where people make a living through farming.”
Noon approached, and it was time for lunch.
Food for reminiscing
Sol-ji’s next destination was the famous open-air Jagalchi seafood market. As she walked from stall to stall, the boisterous calls of merchants mingled together, as they tried to attract customers by shouting out prices in their folksy Busan accents while holding up wriggling fish. Jagalchi is the largest seafood market in the country, and it is another big Busan tourist destination.
Sol-ji looked around the market, carefully observing the fish leaping out of the ice. She seemed to be searching for familiar fish such as flounder, cutlassfish, mackerel, and squid. Although it was an unfamiliar market, the seafood displayed on the stalls was something she often saw back in her hometown, she said.
She recalled how North and South Koreans use different words for squid and two types of octopus and this led to confusion.
문어 (muneo) 낙지 (nakji) 오징어 (ojingeo)
North Korea all octopus varieties squid cuttlefish
South Korea large octopus varieties small octopus varieties squid and cuttlefish
“We called squid nakji . So when I’m here and I see the small octopus that they’re calling nakji , that’s what we used to call baby muneo ,” said Sol-ji.
She recalled that during her childhood she would often snack on dried squid, tearing off tasty parts and chewing it by the mouthful.
The marketplace also conjured up memories of eating raw fish, but the way she enjoyed it up North was very different. In Chongjin raw fish is served slathered in a thick sauce, and wrapped with other ingredients in lettuce. But she was surprised when she came to South Korea and saw people eat the plain white flesh dipped in only a little bit of sauce.
Park Sol-ji visits Jagalchi seafood market in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “I think the seafood I ate in Chongjin was tastier,” she said, smiling broadly. She explained that fish caught in colder places is saltier and tastier.
But then again, she said, it might have just been that she was hungry all the time back then.
“It’s like something out of a dream.”
As the sun set behind Gwangalli Beach, Gwangan Bridge lit up the night sky in a dazzling flash of color. Sol-ji got in line to ride a yacht under the bridge, out to sea to catch the fireworks show exclusively for the passengers.
Park Sol-ji views the city of Busan, South Korea at night off Gwangalli Beach, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) As the yacht moved along, Sol-ji couldn’t help but notice that it was a stark difference from the pitch black nighttime seascape in Chongjin – out at sea, Busan’s night sky is brightly and colorfully illuminated by the bridge, the cityscape – and soon, the fireworks.
Sol-ji sat on the deck, quietly closing her eyes and feeling the sea breeze. Then in one magic moment, lights shot out of the sky with a loud boom. The fireworks brought a bright smile across her face.
In all her excitement, her thoughts drifted to her childhood friends. Although they live in different places now, she thought how wonderful it would be if they could gaze at the dazzling night sea of ​​Busan together.
A yacht tour fireworks display in the waters off Gwangalli Beach in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “This really feels like a dream, but I really do want to try it with them at least once,” she said. “I want to take lots of photos with my friends and go sightseeing like this.”
Under the glowing bursts, she reflected on her current daily life. Nothing like this would ever be possible in North Korea, she said. But in South Korea she can go wherever she wants, with whomever she wants, wearing whatever she wants. She smiled, realizing that “freedom” isn’t a grandiose ideal or political buzzword, it is contained in an ordinary moment like this, on a boat at sea near Busan, under the brightly lit night sky.
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: Harris Ho wins HK's second gold at Youth Olympics
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong, China fencer Harris Ho on Tuesday bagged the city's second gold medal of the Youth Olympics Games in…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong, China fencer Harris Ho on Tuesday bagged the city's second gold medal of the Youth Olympics Games in Senegal, winning the individual men's foil final in dominant fashion.

Ho, the reigning world junior foil champion, defeated Japan's Masashi Maeda 15-8 in the gold medal bout at the Dakar Expo Centre.

The 17-year-old's triumph marks the SAR's first-ever individual fencing gold in the history of the Youth Olympics, with the city having previously claimed two fencing silvers in the 2014 and 2018 editions of the quadrennial event.

Ho's win caps off a dominant run in the competition, going five and one in the group stage to enter the quarter-finals as the second seed.

The SAR star brushed aside the Czech Republic's Krystof Novak 15-2 in the quarter-finals, before beating Cyprus's Aris Kiayias 15-10 in the last four.

The landmark victory also builds on a phenomenal year for Ho, who won the Cadet World Championship title in April, and further cements him as a top contender ahead of the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law congratulated him on capturing gold in Senegal.

"With an outstanding performance at the Youth Olympic Games this year, he overcame his opponents to secure the gold medal and set a historic milestone for a young Hong Kong fencing athlete. All of the Hong Kong citizens take great pride in his remarkable achievement," she said in a statement.

articles.title: Nvidia plunges as tech shares rebound, oil slides
articles.excerpt: US stocks rallied on Monday, as a drop in oil prices tempered inflation fears and helped the S&P 500 rebound…
articles.fullText:
US stocks rallied on Monday, as a drop in oil prices tempered inflation fears and helped the S&P 500 rebound from its biggest weekly drop since April 2025, and tech shares jumped even as AI heavyweight Nvidia slumped with controversy swirling around CEO Jensen Huang.

Last week, stocks slumped after a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections fed concerns that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade.

Markets were in rally mode even as Nvidia, the second-most valuable company in the world, tumbled over 4 percent and closed at its lowest level since April 7. Investors questioned CEO Huang's future at the AI chipmaker after an internal investigation was launched into whether a foreign intelligence effort had targeted him.

China has dismissed the spying allegation as a baseless smear.

"The AI story is not going away if people are worried about that, the Democrats are not going to destroy AI. They can't. It's got a life of its own. They can put regulation around it, but they're certainly not stopping it," said Ken Polcari, partner and chief market strategist at SlateStone Wealth in Jupiter, Florida.

Providing further support was a sharp drop in crude oil prices that helped dampen concerns about price pressures, as US President Donald Trump downplayed the likelihood of renewed strikes on Iran.

"Oil prices for sure, if they're down, that's certainly adding fuel to the fire," said Polcari.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,104 points, or 2.2 percent, to 52,389, the S&P 500 gained 173 points, or 2.4 percent, to 7,549 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 673 points, or 2.7 percent, to 25,253.

The S&P recorded its biggest daily percentage gain since April 8, while the Nasdaq marked its biggest daily advance since July 30.

Inflation readings are on the docket this week as the US Labour Department will release its Consumer Price Index report for October on Tuesday and Producer Price Index on Friday.

Some analysts on Wall Street also viewed last week's decline as an overreaction. Morgan Stanley and UBS said last week's rout in AI stocks was overdone, and risks were low of extreme regulation of data centre developments, even with Democratic majorities in the US Congress.

Even as oil prices have eased, expectations for a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December policy meeting remain above 80 percent, according to CME FedWatch, as October's strong jobs report gave the central bank latitude to continue raising rates.

Chipmakers surged. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index shot up 6.9 percent after plunging more than 12 percent last week, its biggest weekly drop since the week ended April 4, 2025. Nvidia was the sole decliner in the index on Monday, while Broadcom, up 8.8 percent, and Advanced Micro Devices, up 13.3 percent, were the two biggest boosts.

Shares of investment giant KKR advanced 1.7 percent after its quarterly profit hit a record high. Constellation Energy, an energy firm with exposure to the AI buildout, shot up more than 10 percent after its adjusted third-quarter profit surpassed expectations. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
articles.excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox…
articles.fullText:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first,  sign up here .

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.

Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).

The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. 

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.

But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

articles.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
articles.excerpt: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning…
articles.fullText:
As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”

Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”

Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.

Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”

Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.

He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”

Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

articles.title: Harris Ho wins 2nd gold for HK, China
articles.excerpt: Secretary for Culture, Sports & Tourism Rosanna Law today congratulated fencer Harris Ho on winning a gold medal in the…
articles.fullText:
Secretary for Culture, Sports & Tourism Rosanna Law today congratulated fencer Harris Ho on winning a gold medal in the Men's Foil Individual at the 4th Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal.

The victory marks the first gold medal ever won by the Hong Kong, China fencing team at the Games and the second gold medal won by the Hong Kong, China Delegation this year.

Miss Law noted that the triumph adds to Mr Ho's recent string of major successes. Earlier this year, he won a gold medal in the Cadet Boys' Foil Individual (U17) at the 2026 World Junior & Cadet Fencing Championships in April and a silver medal as part of the Men's Foil Team at the Asian Games in September.

“With an outstanding performance at the Youth Olympic Games this year, he overcame his opponents to secure the gold medal and set a historic milestone for a young Hong Kong fencing athlete.

“All Hong Kong citizens take great pride in his remarkable achievement,” Miss Law added.

​The 4th Youth Olympic Games are taking place from October 31 to November 13. Hong Kong sent a total of 15 athletes to compete in 12 sports and has so far won two gold, one silver and three bronze medals.

articles.title: SME business receipts rise slightly
articles.excerpt: The current diffusion index (DI) on business receipts amongst small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) increased slightly from 43.7 in the…
articles.fullText:
The current diffusion index (DI) on business receipts amongst small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) increased slightly from 43.7 in the contractionary zone in September to 43.8 in October, the Census & Statistics Department announced today. Meanwhile, the outlook DI on business receipts for November stood at 46.8.

Analysed by sector, current DIs on business receipts for several surveyed sectors rose in October compared with the previous month, most notably in the import and export trades, which climbed from 43.3 to 44.9. Over the same period, the current DI on new orders for the import and export trades increased from 44.3 in September to 44.6 in October, with the outlook DI for November projected at 47.4.

The Government noted that SME business sentiment remained broadly stable in October, while the overall DI on employment improved for the second consecutive month.

Looking ahead, the Hong Kong economy has performed strongly so far this year and is expected to maintain solid growth, providing continued support for business confidence. However, persistent external uncertainties may continue to affect near-term sentiment, and the Government stated it will monitor the situation closely.

articles.title: Northern Link Project pact signed
articles.excerpt: With the Chief Executive in Council approving the financial arrangement for Part 2 of the Northern Link (NOL) Project today…
articles.fullText:
With the Chief Executive in Council approving the financial arrangement for Part 2 of the Northern Link (NOL) Project today, the Government and the MTR Corporation (MTRC) have executed the agreement for the full NOL Project.

Secretary for Transport & Logistics Mable Chan and the MTRC Chairman Jacob Kim witnessed the representatives of the Transport & Logistics Bureau and the MTRC signing the agreement.

The milestone indicates that the NOL Main Line and Spur Line have fully entered the construction stage, targeting a simultaneous commissioning by 2034 or sooner.

Ms Chan noted that the venture is a strategic railway project under Hong Kong's First Five-Year Plan, actively aligning with the strategies set out in the National 15th Five-Year Plan Outline.

Providing local commuting alongside cross-boundary railway services, the project will open up new transport corridors for both domestic and cross-boundary transit upon its full rollout.

Ms Chan said the project features three highlights - serving the Northern Metropolis, joining two lines, and linking the Greater Bay Area.

“First, the project will serve as the main public transport backbone for several new development areas in the Northern Metropolis including the innovation and technology clusters in the San Tin Technopole and the Loop, driving the expedited development of the Northern Metropolis.

“Secondly, the project will link the Tuen Ma Line and the East Rail Line to form a railway loop, significantly enhancing the coverage and resilience of the railway network.

“Thirdly, the project will connect to the Huanggang Port, thereby integrating the metro networks of Hong Kong and Shenzhen and strengthening infrastructure interconnectivity in the Greater Bay Area.”

To enhance the speed and efficiency of railway development, over the past year the Government and the MTRC teams have taken forward a series of key initiatives to reduce cost and expedite construction.

Ms Chan highlighted that the time for handling building plans has been reduced by 30 to 50%. By implementing the NOL Main Line in combination with the Spur Line as one project, it will also advance the timetable of the Spur Line by two years to commission simultaneously with the Main Line by 2034 or earlier.

The estimated capital cost is verified to be about $54.8 billion. Together with the estimated capital cost for Part 1, the estimated capital cost of the entire NOL Project is about $86.2 billion, which is lower than the original estimate by 28%.

The Chief Executive in Council also approved the grant of sites at Ngau Tam Mei Area 3A, 3D and 4A; San Tin Area 2A and 2G; Kwu Tung North Area 23 and 26 (East); as well as part of the site for residential use in the proposed Au Tau New Development Area, to the MTRC for residential and commercial development under the "Rail-plus-Property" model.

The NOL Main Line involves the construction of a 10.7-kilometre-long underground railway and five stations. There will be two interchange stations at Kam Sheung Road Station and Kwu Tung Station connecting with the Tuen Ma Line and the East Rail Line respectively, as well as three intermediate stations at San Tin, Ngau Tam Mei and Au Tau.

Upon commissioning, the travelling time between Kam Sheung Road and Kwu Tung during peak hours will be significantly reduced from the current 60 minutes to 12 minutes.

The Spur Line involves the construction of an underground railway of about 6 kilometres in length branching off from San Tin Station on the NOL Main Line, of which the Shenzhen section is approximately 1.1 kilometres long.

There will be three new stations, including intermediate stations at Chau Tau and the Loop, as well as the terminal at the Huanggang Port in Shenzhen. The travelling time between San Tin and the Huanggang Port is expected to be only about 11 minutes upon commissioning.

articles.title: Disney, Adobe strike deal to co-develop AI models
articles.excerpt: Disney and Adobe have struck a multi-year deal to co-develop custom generative AI models for the media giant with the…
articles.fullText:
Disney and Adobe have struck a multi-year deal to co-develop custom generative AI models for the media giant with the goal of scaling AI tools across its theme parks, studio and sports media businesses.

The move, announced on Monday, will start with speeding up project development timelines at Disney's Experiences division, home to its global theme parks, resorts and cruise lines, and for concept exploration at StudioLAB, the innovation hub within Walt Disney Studios.

Adobe will also work with Disney to use AI tools to boost engagement with sports fans at ESPN and bring more of ESPN's content archive to audiences.

Through Adobe's Firefly Foundry, which lets enterprises build and deploy custom AI models, the two companies will work on gen-AI models trained on Disney's intellectual properties that will generate production-ready outputs. The models will be private and proprietary to Disney.

Walt Disney Imagineering, the creative, design, and research and development arm behind Disney Experiences, has deployed a custom image generation model and a sketch-to-image model that can turn hand-drawn sketches into fully-rendered concept art.

"We talk about the time frames in our projects in years – it's years' worth of development. And what Adobe Foundry has allowed us to do is compress the creative process that would have taken months to now being able to do that in hours and days," Kyle Laughlin, senior vice president of R&D technology and engineering at Disney, said in an interview.

"We're able to run through multiple iterations quickly with these tools. And that helps us reduce costly changes in the field once we get into the construction of these experiences," Laughlin said, adding that the tools will help accelerate creative development at Disney and are "in no way meant to replace" roles at Imagineering.

Earlier this month, Bloomberg News reported that Disney was considering cutting thousands of jobs and has asked some managers to target 20 percent in annual cost savings. (Reuters)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: The Download: empty AI climate claims, and an Nvidia investigation
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made 

—By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm

This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising.  Read the full story .

Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests  

Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction.

The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree.

For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide.

Learn more about Dent, her work, and her impact on how we understand the role rainforests play in regulating our climate.

—Matthew Ponsford

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Nvidia is investigating its own boss
Jensen Huang has admitted to intimacy with a suspected Chinese spy. ( NYT $)
+ Shares in Nvidia were down 5% in pre-market trading. ( CNBC )
+ Huang’s children are also employed by Nvidia. ( WSJ $)

2 Democrats are planning a blitz of investigations into Big Tech
Reportedly starting with Apple, Meta, and Musk’s companies. ( WP $)
+ They’re hoping to harness the data center backlash to rein in the AI sector. ( Vox $)
+ Here’s why the midterms sparked an AI stock selloff. ( BBC )

3 The UN annual climate meeting starts today
It’s the first to be held after confirmation the planet will exceed 1.5 °C warming. ( Nature )
+ How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Connecting fridges to the internet looks like a bad move now
We still don’t know who is behind recent hacks, or even if they’re connected. ( The Atlantic $)
+ Experts say they should be a “wake up call” for the industry. ( NPR )
+ Are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic? ( The Guardian )
+ AI is already making online crimes easier. It could get much worse. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 Tesla is axing the Cybertruck
RIP, we hardly knew ye. ( Wired $)
+ The Cybertruck was on our “worst tech flops of 2025” list. ( MIT Technology Review )

6 Iran might attack subsea cables if the US escalates again
That’s the message it’s sending via several loitering tankers. ( FT $)

7 Chinese AI labs are struggling to poach Silicon Valley workers
Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot have an uphill battle as they try to fill new US offices. ( Rest of World )
+ China’s AI models have Trump’s AI world at war with itself. ( MIT Technology Review )

8 Online piracy is back
But this time, archivist zeal is at least as big a draw as accessing content for free. ( The Verge )
+ Inside the race to save our online lives from a digital dark age. ( MIT Technology Review )

9 How do you land on a moon with almost no gravity?
It’s a huge challenge to land on Martian moon Phobos—here’s how Japan’s going to attempt it. ( IEEE Spectrum )

10 Meet Philadelphia’s delivery robot saboteur
Carolyn Marvin is going to court for blocking them, and it’s turning her into a local hero. ( The Guardian )

Quote of the day

“Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility.” 

—Jensen Huang apologizes to Nvidia employees for his affair with a suspected Chinese spy in a mass email sent yesterday, the  Washington Post  reports.

One more thing

STUART BRADFORD

AI is coming for music, too

AI models are marching into a creative field that is uniquely vulnerable to disruption: music.

AI-generated creative works—from orchestra performances to heavy metal—are poised to suffuse our lives more thoroughly than any other product of AI has done yet.

The songs are likely to blend into our streaming platforms, party and wedding playlists, soundtracks, and more, whether or not we notice who (or what) made them.

Here’s why AI is set to forever change how we make music.

—James O’Donnell

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ French bardcore band Corseval has given ABBA  a medieval makeover .
+ A stunning  collection of prehistoric engravings  has been found in a Spanish cave.
+  This browser game  flips a retro classic on its head: you control the asteroids, not the spaceship.
+ From a caiman in a wig to a leopard doing a handstand, the  Comedy Wildlife Awards  shortlist is a delight.

articles.title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
articles.excerpt: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new…
articles.fullText:
